candidate: MICI-PE-2015-0094 Rural Land Titling PTRT-3, Peruvian Amazon
reason: not yet researched: MICI 2024 report frames deforestation and titling harms as potential
r16_note: Fails test 2, and the drop is confirmed on an independent read. I downloaded the MICI Compliance Review Report for PTRT-3 (PE-L1026, loan 3370/OC-PE) from https://www.iadb.org/document.cfm?id=EZIDB0000559-1009163277-2745 and extracted 4,349 lines of text. I read the determination paragraphs 2.148, 2.152, 2.156, 2.160 and 2.163 and the whole 'Harm' block of the conclusions, and searched the full text for 'displaced', 'lost their land', 'invasion', 'evict', 'killed', 'death' and 'threat'. Every harm heading in the conclusions is hedged: 'Potential harm related to shortcomings in the consultation processes' ('may have made it impossible', 'could have prevented'); 'Potential harm related to inadequate categorization' ('may have played a role'); and 'Harm related to the inadequate identification of socioenvironmental risks' ('may have intensified the vulnerability of the lands, environment, health, and culture'). The only unhedged consequence is under 'Potential harm related to failure to meet targets for titling Native communities': the failure to meet titling targets 'led to frustration, disillusionment, and a sense of having been deceived', 'causing to maintain the legal insecurity of tenure over their territories' and undermining confidence in the IDB. That is a benefit not delivered and a pre-existing insecurity left in place, not land, income, health, liberty or life lost. The violence the report does describe - at least 15 Indigenous leaders murdered in Peru's Amazon since 2013, and threats and assassination attempts against AIDESEP - is in section 1.5, 'Context of violence in the Peruvian Amazon', and is attributed to illegal loggers, miners and illicit crops; Management's own comment on the draft report says that section sets out the geographic and social context. The two deaths at line 762 are from the 2020 political crisis, sourced to Human Rights Watch, and are not project-related. Nothing in the report records project-caused harm that happened.

candidate: IRM RQ 2010/2 Medupi coal plant, Lephalale
reason: not yet researched: IRM found partial compliance on air, water and graves; on-the-ground harm not established in pages read
r16_note: Cut on test 2: nothing in the documents records harm that happened. I opened the IRM Compliance Review of 19 December 2011 (https://aconsole-static.s3.amazonaws.com/media/public/cases/CR_Report.pdf, 2,446 lines of text) and the fifth monitoring report of 28 January 2022 (https://aconsole-static.s3.amazonaws.com/media/public/cases/medupi_monitor_5.pdf, 747 lines), and read the Water Access, Land and Water Degradation, Consultation and Issues of Graves sections in full. (1) The land and water finding is a hedge, not a finding of damage: 'It is important to note that the evidence of water and land degradation, if it occurs, will not be clear until the power plant is operational. Consequently, it is not possible to reach a firm conclusion about Bank compliance with the applicable policies before Medupi becomes operational.' The whole discussion is of risk - the ash dump 'could leach', 'there may be greater risk from particulate matter', 'the community is anxious' - and the IRM says the validity of the air-quality concern 'is difficult to evaluate in the absence of a strong research base'. (2) The sand mining strand does not carry the case. The compliance report mentions the Mokolo River only as the Requestors' allegation of 'allegedly unlawful sand dredging'. The phrase 'damage done to Mokolo River' that the draft was built on appears only in the IRM Second Monitoring Findings column of the monitoring table, in a sentence whose claim is procedural: an environmental assessment done for a sand mining licence application 'could not substitute for an independent assessment of the damage done to Mokolo River and the rehabilitation requirements by previous legal and illegal sand mining operations'. The damage needing assessment is attributed there to previous legal and illegal sand mining, not to the Medupi works, and the Fourth Monitoring Findings record that the Department of Mineral Resources handled and closed the matter, concluding that Eskom 'could not be responsible for the rehabilitation of all mined areas'. The action is marked completed. (3) The monitoring report's own water finding runs the other way, and the draft omitted it: at action 3.3 the IRM's second and third monitoring findings both say 'Water quality appears not to have been affected by the construction of the Medupi Plant. Water quality is being adequately monitored by Eskom.' (4) The graves finding is a finding about the Bank and about risk, not a record of desecration: the Panel finds the Bank 'was not sufficiently rigorous in its assessment of this policy to determine either that no graves had been or could have been desecrated by the Medupi project or that the borrower had established adequate procedures to consult'. No grave is recorded as desecrated. Management's position is confirmed as drafted - two graves on the site, one an old grave with an affidavit showing it had not been visited since 1967, which Eskom relocated to a formal cemetery following the appropriate legal procedures, and the grave of a child whose mother had agreed in principle but was being prevented from signing - and the fifth monitoring report records remediation: a heritage assessment, graves identified on the Medupi site, cleansing and appeasement ceremonies, and a memorial site. Remediation is not harm. The single relocation in the compliance report is the one full-time worker on one of the purchased farms, 'relocated, with his consent, by the owner of this farm to one of his other properties' - consented, and done by the farm owner. (5) The emissions figures are accurate but document non-compliance with licence limits, not harm, and the draft said so itself. I opened Eskom's annual emissions report for April 2025 to March 2026 and confirmed every figure: 12 SO2 exceedances of the 3,500 mg/Nm3 monthly limit, all at Unit 4 in February 2026 and 'All the exceedances were due to the faulty CEMS'; 40 PM exceedances of the 50 mg/Nm3 daily limit, of which 22 were within start-up and shutdown grace, 12 were due to faulty CEMS and 6 were reported as section 30 incidents; 12 NOx readings above 750 mg/Nm3, also 'due to faulty CEMS'; and on ambient air, 'There were no exceedances of the PM10 daily limit, the SO2 daily limit and the NO2 hourly limit recorded during 2025 monitoring period', with the area non-compliant only on ozone, which Eskom attributes to multiple sources including neighbouring third parties. Of 20 dust fall-out buckets, 18 recorded no exceedances; D15a exceeded the 1,200 mg/m2/day non-residential limit 6 times, peaking at 4,645 in October 2025, and D5a 3 times, peaking at 3,979. (6) That report also fails test 3 independently. It covers 2025-26, and the IRM's fifth monitoring report says the project 'has already been fully disbursed and therefore, there is little leverage on the part the Bank to influence the borrower', and that the IRM decided 'to suspend the annual monitoring until at least 2026'. The AfDB money was gone and the Bank no longer supervised when those readings were taken. Because the case is cut, the draft's 'wb' lender key was not pursued; the World Bank's US$3.75 billion Eskom Investment Support Project loan and Inspection Panel case 65 were not verified against a World Bank document during this check. There is no existing Medupi case in cases.json, so this is a drop, not a duplicate. If the owner wants a Medupi case later, the thing to look for is a document that records harm having occurred - a health study, a court finding, or a water or soil result - because the IRM and the Inspection Panel both stopped at risk.

candidate: Nenskra Hydropower, Georgia, CRP 2017/4
reason: CRP found prima facie non-compliance and likely harm for a project ADB was still considering; no documented on-ground harm. Not yet researched further.
r16_note:
Fails tests 2 and 3: no construction, so no harm. A 2024 NGO report filed to the Council of Europe (rm.coe.int, the Svaneti/Nenskra complainants' report, which I read in full at about 1,400 words) records that local people say work has not started on Nenskra and that no construction company had been selected, with the government saying it expected works to resume 'by the end of the year, 2024 at the latest'. OC Media (2020) records that construction has been on hold since Salini Impregilo left in October 2018, and that Bankwatch's field investigation found over 200 people 'would lose' homes, land or pastures — future loss. Bankwatch's own September 2017 blog says pasture and wooden cabins 'would be temporarily or permanently lost' and records no confirmed loss. The EBRD and EIB complaint mechanisms found the project non-compliant with their standards on land acquisition, resettlement, economic displacement, Indigenous issues, cultural heritage, disclosure and engagement, but those are findings about the banks, not records of harm, and neither bank had signed its loan agreement (EBRD $214 million, EIB $150 million, both approved). ADB is listed only as a prospective investor. One item I could not open: business-humanrights.org's summary of a later NGO report saying JSC Nenskra Hydro failed to provide adequate compensation for people affected — both the English and French URLs returned a client error from the site and nothing of either page was retrieved, so whether land was in fact acquired is unresolved and someone should retry that page.

CHECKER: drop confirmed, and the open question closed. The business-humanrights.org page the writer could not open does open: fetched with an ordinary browser user-agent it returns HTTP 200, not a client error. It is dated 10 October 2017, not later, and it is only a pointer to the same Bankwatch report plus a company response from JSC Nenskra Hydro. I then downloaded and read in full the underlying report itself, Bankwatch's 'Failing local communities: Report on the Land Assessment and Livelihoods Restoration Plan for the Nenskra Hydropower Project', September 2017, 9,138 words. Every loss in it is prospective: households 'would lose' compensation, 'will lose' access and income, and the pastures and cabins are described as being inside the 'land take area'. It records no completed acquisition and no completed loss. Nothing is left to retry on this lead.

candidate: Assam Solar Project, Karbi Anglong, CRP 2024/8 and 2025/3
reason: India withdrew the ADB loan request in May 2025 before any compliance review; alleged displacement of Karbi households not documented by an independent source read. Not yet researched.
r16_note:
Fails tests 2 and 3. PUCL's account of the Karbi people's struggle (pucl.org, read in full) describes the 18,000 bighas in East Karbi Anglong as land that 'would be taken up', the 24 villages and more than 20,000 people as those who 'would be directly affected', and residents' fear of losing their homes; it reports no crop losses, no fencing, no evictions and no arrests, and names no fact-finding team's findings on the ground. ADB withdrew the $434.25 million loan request in May 2025 before approval, so no ADB money was in place when anything could have happened; PUCL's own postscript records the withdrawal and says the struggle to cancel the project continues. PUCL also gives the loan as both $435.25 million and $434.25 million and does not explain the gap. A separate report that India's National Commission for Scheduled Tribes has sought a report on the 18,000 bighas after the cancellation was seen only as a headline and not opened.

CHECKER: drop confirmed from ADB's own document, which the writer did not have. ADB's Accountability Mechanism Annual Report 2025 records for the Assam Solar Project second complaint that the Compliance Review Panel 'found preliminary evidence of noncompliance in several areas' and 'recommended that the Board authorize a compliance review. However, after the Government of India formally withdrew its request for ADB financing, the complaint no longer related to an ADB-financed project and fell outside the compliance review mandate.' That is a hedged preliminary finding about the lender, with no ADB money ever in place, so tests 1, 2 and 3 all fail.

candidate: Georgian Railway Green Bond (Zestaponi–Kharagauli–Khashuri landslides), CRP 2025/9
reason: Complaint alleges over 100 families displaced by landslides; CRP found it non-admissible. Not yet researched.
r16_note:
Fails the link test, on the office's own words. The harm is real and documented: Democracy and Freedom Watch reports a roughly three-kilometre rupture across the mountainside at Khemaghali and Ghverki in Kharagauli municipality, first noticed as cracks on 26 May 2025, with about 107 households in the two villages before the slide, most told to leave and rent elsewhere, most homes in Khemaghali abandoned with cracked walls, government rent support of up to 500 lari a month and many villagers left off the registries. But the Compliance Review Panel found the complaint outside the scope of compliance review because the alleged harms were not related to ADB-financed components, stating that 'The construction of the tunnels falls strictly outside the activities financed by ADB' — ADB's $20 million in Georgian Railway green bonds since 2021 went to substation renovation, bridges, culverts, track laying, electrification and water works, not tunnelling (Sakartvelos Ambebi, reporting the Panel's decision). Residents say experts privately linked the slide to blasting for railway construction in 2019–2022; no official geological finding on the cause has been published. If a future document ties the blasting to an ADB-financed component, this becomes a case.

CHECKER: drop confirmed, and the Panel's reasoning now comes from ADB rather than from press reporting of it. ADB's Accountability Mechanism Annual Report 2025 states: 'Following initial assessment and review of project documentation, the CRP determined that the complaint was not admissible. The CRP found that ADB financing had not been used for new railway lines or tunnel-related works, and that the alleged impacts related to activities outside the scope of ADB financing.' ADB's complaint register gives the complaint as 2025-118, received 17 October 2025, project 55132-001, forwarded to the CRP on 7 November 2025. The link test fails on the office's own words.

r16_note: Cut on test 2: a grievance that was settled, not documented harm. I downloaded and read in full ADB's Final Report of the Special Project Facilitator for SPF-2019-12-03-0092 (October 2023, 2,340 words, project 36173-013, loans 2557 and 2558). It is one household. The only payment tied to the house is SLRs121,000, paid by the Colombo Municipal Council on 5 December 2017, which the report calls 'the estimated cost of repair works directly related to his house' — a repair estimate, not a survey of damage. No document records what the damage was: the report names no street, no ward, no cracks, no structural finding and no number of affected houses, and where it refers to damage at all it is as the complainants' claim ('They alleged that they were entitled to further compensation for construction damage'). The project fact sheet in the same report says the works were limited to upgrading existing sewerage inside existing facilities and that the project 'will not require permanent or temporary land acquisition and there will be no impact on permanent structures or other assets'. The health claim was rejected by the council as not caused by construction; the contractor's insurer paid 75 per cent of the medical costs and the council the remaining SLRs41,852.33 after a Grievance Redress Committee meeting on 26 November 2018. By the time the case closed, ADB's Special Project Facilitator had found that 'almost all the requests of complainants for payment relating to the impact of the Project on their property and well-being have already been paid and/or have been approved by CMC' and had advised the complainants that the council's final offer 'appeared to be consistent with ADB policies'; the complainants did not accept it, the council declined further problem-solving and the office closed the case. The two earlier complaints, SPF-2017-04-01-0061 and SPF-2018-10-02-0079, were found ineligible and carry no findings on the facts. Also verified for the merge question: ADB's project page for 36173-013 lists loans 2557-SRI (US$80.00 million, ordinary capital resources) and 2558-SRI and gives cofinancing of 0.00, so there is no EIB money in this project.

r16_note:
Fails test 2 on what I could open: the harm is feared, not recorded. ADB's complaint page for SPF-2022-14-02-0134 (filed 11 October 2022, found eligible 5 December 2022, review and assessment report issued 13 January 2025) lists only issue categories — resettlement, compensation and valuation; noise and vibration; easement rights, environment and safety. Twenty-four apartments in three blocks were first notified for acquisition and, after the alignment was revised, eight 'were to be acquired'; the other sixteen households were excluded. Specialists hired by ADB's office found the chosen alignment 'the least harmful and within the policy framework' against ADB's 2009 Safeguard Policy Statement, Indian courts upheld the decision and an appeal was dismissed, and a February 2024 memorandum with eight of the sixteen households provided temporary relocation support, a baseline structural stability survey funded by ADB's office and a commitment to repair verified damage, with pre-construction surveys done for 14 of the 16 apartments by June 2024. Measures to catch damage if it happens are not damage. The ADB publication 'A Rail Too Far?' (June 2025, 16 pages) would be the place to check: its landing page served only metadata, abstract and contents, and the PDF itself was not opened. If its text records damage found by those surveys, this becomes a case.

CHECKER: drop confirmed against the one document the writer named but did not open. I downloaded ADB's publication 'A Rail Too Far? India's Delhi–Meerut Regional Rapid Transit System Investment Project Complaint' and read it in full, 3,410 words. It records no damage found. The structural work in it is a baseline survey only: an independent structural engineer was brought in 'to conduct a baseline survey to assess the structural stability of the homes before the beginning' of works, pre-construction surveys of 14 of the 16 apartments had been done, and the company 'agreed to fix any damage reported by the experts after construction'. On land, the publication says the company initially declared 24 apartments as needing to be purchased, that after the alignment changed only eight 'needed to be acquired', and that the company reached agreements with three of those eight. No completed acquisition, no completed move and no recorded damage, so test 2 fails.

candidate: ipam:2018/08 Nenskra hydropower, Svaneti (Georgia)
reason: not yet researched: compliance review found five non-compliances including livelihood restoration, but construction was halted and EBRD withdrew; harm on the ground not yet documented
r16_note: Dropped on tests 2 and 3. The draft kept this on a land grant of about 700 hectares and on unpaid pasture and cabin compensation. I opened the single source that carries the harm, CEE Bankwatch Network's report of 11 September 2017 (https://bankwatch.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/Nenskra-LALRP-11Sep2017.pdf), and it is written in the future and conditional throughout: "PAPs in these areas will be mainly affected by the temporary or permanent loss of pastures", a household "will be permanently affected by loss of pasture land and a wooden cabin at Mashrichala", "who will lose access to the Kvemo Memuli pasture area", and "these households would lose access" to cabins. Its field work was two visits, 1-5 and 17-19 July 2017, and 20 households. The draft had promoted these to completed losses, writing that access to cabins "is lost". The report says no compensation agreements had been signed - "This has not happened, but it is unclear what the new timeline is" - so there were offers outstanding for losses that had not yet occurred, not compensation owed for land people had already lost. The grant of 96.2 hectares in Chuberi for USD 1 and 600.0252 hectares for 55 years is a transfer on paper to the project company; nothing I opened records anyone losing the use of that land. The EIB Complaints Mechanism conclusions report of 7 February 2020 (https://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2018-32-nenskra-hpp-cr-3-06-2020-docx.pdf) does not state whether any land was transferred, acquired or occupied and does not state whether any compensation was paid, owed or withheld; the words LALRP, pastures, cabins and Kvemo Memuli do not appear in it. Its findings are about the Bank - no documented assessment under EIB Standard 7, "no evidence that the Bank took the adequate steps to assure itself of the proper application of Standard 7", an ADB vulnerability approach "very different from the definition of vulnerability in EIB Standard 7", a labour influx assessment "insufficient at this time" - and a finding against the lender is not harm. On timing: the NGO report to the Bern Convention of 12 February 2024 (https://rm.coe.int/files18e-2024-georgia-svaneti-nenskra-ngo-rep/1680aebea7) says "Local people informed us that work on none of the three projects has started yet" and "To the best of our knowledge, none has a construction company selected". Bankwatch's status update of 9 April 2020 (https://bankwatch.org/blog/status-update-on-the-nenskra-hydropower-plant-project) says activity "remains at a standstill", that the company abandoned the project "before construction had even begun", and that local sources said "almost all preparatory works have been stopped"; it records unpaid wages to local employees, not resident compensation. The EBRD IPAM case registry entry (https://www.ebrd.com/home/what-we-do/projects/independent-project-accountability-mechanism/case-registry/nenskra-hpp.html) gives a Monitoring Closing Report of 24 June 2026 stating "IPAM has been informed by Management that the Project has been cancelled" and that "the remaining open MAP actions are project-specific in nature", with obligations to be reactivated if the project is revived, materially restructured or resubmitted to the EBRD Board. So the project was cancelled before construction, and the preparation exception does not apply because no land take, tree felling, pasture loss or household move is documented anywhere I opened. ITEM I COULD NOT OPEN: business-humanrights.org's summary of an NGO report saying JSC Nenskra Hydro failed to compensate affected people. https://www.business-humanrights.org/en/latest-news/georgia-new-ngo-report-says-jsc-nenskra-hydro-fails-to-provide-adequate-compensation-for-people-affected-by-its-hydropower-plant-company-responds returned only site navigation and the headline, no body text; the French path https://business-humanrights.org/fr/dernieres-actualites/georgia-new-ngo-report-says-jsc-nenskra-hydro-fails-to-provide-adequate-compensation-for-people-affected-by-its-hydropower-plant-company-responds and https://www.bhrrc.org/ru/... both failed at the site with a client error. Neither is a host block. Searching for the underlying NGO report returned the same cluster of business-humanrights.org locale pages plus the 11 September 2017 Bankwatch report and its companion blog of the same date (https://bankwatch.org/blog/systematic-shortcomings-will-deprive-people-affected-by-georgian-dam-of-compensation), which I opened: it too says only that compensation "was offered" and "has been miscalculated", and describes cabins "that would be temporarily or permanently lost". That blog's own title is future tense. On the evidence I could reach, the business-humanrights item appears to summarise the 2017 Bankwatch report rather than a later one, so it would not add an independent source even if it opened. FIGURE PAIRS, for the record, each as its source states it and neither reconciled by anything I read: K-water's stake in JSC Nenskra Hydro is 85% per the EIB report of 7 February 2020, which gives no date label for the shareholding, and 80% per OC Media (2018); the EBRD is a 5% equity holder per that EIB report and a USD 214 million lender with a board date of 31 January 2018 and status "Approved" per the Early Warning System record for EBRD-46778. LENDER LIST, checked as asked: of the five institutions claimed, only two are documented as actually in. The EIB report puts the EIB's own loan of up to USD 150 million as approved on 6 February 2018 with status "Pending signature", and the 2024 NGO report says the EBRD and EIB loans of USD 214 million and USD 150 million "remain approved". The EIB report's footnote 1 names ADB, EBRD, KDB, AIIB and K-sure only as the "potential Lenders" as at November 2017, and the Early Warning System record for ADB-49223-001 lists the project as "Proposed". So ADB and AIIB are documented as potential or proposed only, and the draft's claim of five institutions on this project does not hold. K-water, 85% owner of the project company and itself 91.5% state-owned per the Early Warning System, is a real foreign owner, and the EBRD's 5% equity is real money in, so test 1 would pass; the case fails on tests 2 and 3. ALSO CORRECTED FROM THE DRAFT: the EBRD case page (https://www.ebrd.com/work-with-us/projects/ipam/2018/08.html) gives a registration date of 30 May 2018 with the Request document dated 11 June 2018, not a registration on 11 June 2018; the requesters are described as residents of four community members of Chuberi; and that page shows "Confidentiality Request: No" while its summary says they asked for their identities to be kept confidential, which the registry entry records as "Requested". The other agent working the ADB side of the same project dropped it too, so Nenskra now appears nowhere, and the one-case rule is satisfied.

candidate: eibcm:Malawi NRWB water efficiency (Malawi)
reason: not yet researched: property damage in three northern communities, settled by agreements in 2022
r16_note: Cut from the draft. Causation is not established for the house damage, and no document records land actually taken. I opened both monitoring reports. The final monitoring report for Chipambo and Geisha of 15 December 2022 (https://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2021-16a-chipambo-geisha-malawi-nrwb-water-efficiency-final-monitoring-report-2022-12-15.pdf) makes no finding on causation. It describes the promoter's approach as "to assess the damage to structures of the households concerned, evaluate the cost and then make the payment", and the payments as made under the promoter's "standing offer to pay", with no causal finding attached. In the one strand that was actually tested, the owner and the promoter jointly chose an independent engineer who found it "cannot be established" that the excavation works caused the damage, and both parties accepted that. Under the brief, a payment for assessed damage with no admission is a settlement without admission and does not establish the harm; here it is weaker still, because the only engineering test performed found against causation. The second monitoring report on Kazando of 15 March 2024 (https://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2021-16a-second-monitoring-report-kazando-malawi-nrwb-water-efficiency.pdf) likewise does not attribute the damage to the works: its only wording is "the damage to structures" and "the damaged structures in question". Neither report says any land was taken or occupied by the works. They record valuations and compensation payments - 234 households assessed, 231 signing on 6 July 2022, the finalised valuation report submitted by the Regional Commissioner for Lands North on 11 July 2022, 219 community members paid between 26 August and 21 September 2022 - but no description of land take, of what was lost, or of any amount. Compensation that was late and then paid is not documented harm; the writer dropped the Tunisian G1 Penetrante Sud lead on the same ground. TWO SOURCING ERRORS IN THE DRAFT, both corrected by reading the reports. First, the collapsed house: the report's wording is "One refused to receive payment because allegedly his house collapsed." That is the office's own sentence with the word "allegedly" in it, not the household's own statement as the draft said, and the draft quoted the clause with "allegedly" removed. Second, the draft said "The office's second monitoring report says the household counts of 13, 14, 15 and 17 differ across its own sections and does not reconcile them." The report says no such thing. It simply uses the different counts - "payment of the remaining compensation to 13 households", "the draft valuation report for the 14 missing households", "the Promoter made the payments to 15 households" with "Two households had already been paid previously", and "paid compensation to the 17 affected members of the community" - without reconciling them. The observation is the writer's, attributed to the office. The counts are accurate as quoted and the lack of reconciliation is real; there is a further unreconciled pair the draft missed, between the "two additional communal water points" in action 4 and the "request for additional three communal water points" in its status note. Other figures I checked and found accurate: the 20 of 38 paid on 13 December 2022, the assessment of 23 September to 3 October 2022 disclosed on 19 October 2022, the 11 objections over cracks "not included in the assessment of the damage", the three unavailable and three engaging a private valuer, the 17 members paid on 4 August 2022, the 15 households paid on 26 August 2022, the three water points finished by March 2023, the MWK 47 million estimate for the health centre at end 2023 and the promoter's figure of 22 new household connections by December 2023. The reports give no amounts paid for anything. The EIB loan of up to EUR 24.6 million approved in November 2016, the total cost of EUR 60.4 million and the Northern Region Water Board as promoter are all confirmed; the 15 December 2022 report does not give the signature date. The second complaint SG/E/2024/07 is a consultant's unpaid contract dispute, which the brief excludes.

candidate: eibcm:Tunisian roads and rail (S2 Sfax, Réseau Ferroviaire Rapide, Autoroute du Centre, G1, X4, S4 Zarzis, Sfax-Gabès)
reason: not yet researched: expropriation and business-loss complaints
r16_note: Cut from the draft. The one case written from this lead, rfr-bardo-expropriation-tunis, does not stand. The property at Bardo was never taken into possession, no compensation was ever paid, and the office found the compensation allegations not grounded. I read the conclusions report of 27 January 2020 in full, in two passes covering characters 0-100,000 and 99,000 to the end of its 112,012 characters (http://www.eib.org/attachments/complaints/sg-e-2016-04-rfr-conclusions-report-en-27-01-2020.pdf), which closes the gap the writer left. The decisive point, which the draft missed: possession was not taken. Section 5.7 records the promoter awaiting execution of the decision to take possession, and the Court of First Instance dismissed the Public Prosecutor's demand to take possession on 26 June 2014. A later decision of 23 October 2017 concerned a challenge to an order of 17 May 2017 that possession should be taken; the court rejected the appeal on the merits but said it could not rule on the validity of the expropriation procedure. Nowhere in the report - and I looked specifically in the closing sections - does it say the land was occupied or used by the works, that the complainant lost the use of it, or that any compensation was paid. The promoter offered 250 dinars/m2 and then 400 dinars/m2; the complainant refused both and the file went to court. So the draft's title, "half a property taken at Bardo in 2014", is not supported: there is an expropriation decree of 7 January 2014, and the sentence "only half of the complainant's land was expropriated" is the EIB services' description of what that decree covered, which the draft turned into a completed land loss. What the office concluded is conditional or against itself. On compensation adequacy it found the allegation "not grounded in the context of EIB's obligations", said the amount offered in 2014 may be affected by elapsed time and inflation and that the project "may have a negative impact on the complainant's right on the expropriated land", and said the 2014 amount was likely inadequate only "if not addressed through a process of recalculation". Refusal to expropriate the remaining land was "not grounded" because the remainder exceeded the 25 per cent threshold; refusal to compensate in kind was "not grounded"; the cultural heritage allegation was "not grounded". The one grounded finding is stakeholder engagement, where the office found Tunisian EIA law lacks public consultation provisions and that this had "a tangible negative impact on the local ownership of the Project" - a finding about the Bank and the national framework, not harm to a person. The general observation that in Tunisia "the compensation amounts offered are very low and it is often necessary to go to court" is, as suspected, what EIB services told the office about the country, not about this complainant, and with the individual loss gone it would have been carrying the case. The counts of 31 expropriation procedures on line D in September 2016, 95 pending files in March 2015 with 69 referring to "land that is not in use at all", and 29 cases awaiting judgment in November 2018 are files, not people, and 69 of the 95 are on unused land. Verified and accurate as quoted but carrying no harm: the 2013 waiver (the EIB decided in July 2013 to conditionally waive the satisfactory Resettlement Action Plan condition for first disbursement, and first disbursement was made on 9 September 2013), the loan of up to EUR 177 million approved 21 October 2009 and signed 10 December 2010, AFD as leading institution with KfW and the European Commission (NIF) as co-financiers with no amounts given, the Bardo municipal council's unanimous decision in March 2019 on the temporary stop of works (reported by national press, and 16 council members resigned by the end of that month), and the recommendations with EIB services to report to the Management Committee during 2020 and the office to monitor by the first quarter of 2021. One draft quote was not verbatim: the court's reason reads "the first of the defendants, i.e. the first individual identified in the Expropriation Decree, was deceased". DEDUPE, as asked: this is not a duplicate of the existing case sfax-rocade-interchanges. That case is the Modernisation Routiere II road loan at the Sfax km 4 ring road, complaints SG/E/2018/43 and SG/E/2021/03, about 240 km away; this lead was the EUR 177 million Reseau Ferroviaire Rapide rail loan in Tunis, complaint SG/E/2016/04. Different project, different loan, different place. The question is moot now that the entry is cut. The rest of lead 24 - the five other Tunisian stretches - the writer dropped with the pages it opened, and those reasons are recorded in the lead_notes entry for lead 24 in this file. I did not re-open them; on the writer's own account each stops at a likelihood, a settled compensation dispute or no finding on causation, which is consistent with what I found in the Bardo report.

candidate: eibcm:Greater Colombo wastewater, Narahenpita (Sri Lanka)
reason: not yet researched: house damage and odour; friendly solution
r16_note: Drop upheld. I opened the dispute resolution report of 30 June 2025 (https://www.eib.org/files/complaints/2025-06-30PUBLIC-Disputeresolutionreport-SG-E-2024-27GreaterColomboWastewaterProject.pdf) and it records expected damage only. The 37 households of Narahenpita were concerned that the works "may cause damage to the surrounding houses" and "may cause land subsidence" near the site, and about "unpleasant smells", mosquito infestation and other health risks. The report records no actual damage to any house, no actual odour, no land subsidence and nobody actually moved; the agreed relocation is described as future steps, with residents to submit rental agreements and vacate after payment. Excavation for the Narahenpita pumping station began in September 2024 and the report says construction "generally progressed peacefully" after the October 2024 joint session, with completion planned for September 2026. The friendly solution entitles 23 owners of first-row housing units to a temporary relocation package of monthly rent for 12 months and transport costs, paid in four instalments; second-row residents are to be relocated only if structural stability is at risk, with minor damage repaired in place; and the promoter will coordinate with the Urban Development Authority on apartments for first-row owners, with assurance letters expected by July 2025, while saying it cannot guarantee relocation for interested second-row residents. All forward-looking, so test 2 fails. EIB financing confirmed: approved financing of EUR 50 million on 19 May 2016, finance contract signed 20 January 2017, borrower "the Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka", promoter the Colombo Municipal Council. MERGE ANSWER, as asked. The EIB loan does NOT belong on the other agent's ADB case for project 36173-013. The dispute resolution report does not mention the ADB at all and does not describe the project as part of a wider programme, so it gives no basis for attaching the EIB to any ADB project. The EIB's own project sheet for 20140457 does (https://eib.org/en/projects/all/20140457): its description begins "As part of the Greater Colombo Water and Wastewater Management Improvement Investment Program", and the sheet says that programme was "initiated by the Asian Development Bank (ADB)". That named programme is ADB 45148, Greater Colombo Water and Wastewater Management Improvement Investment Program, which is a different and separately numbered operation from ADB 36173-013, the Greater Colombo Wastewater Management Project. The sheet also shows the signature as EUR 50,000,000 on 20/01/2017 plus a EUR 8,500,000 European Commission investment grant, EUR 58.5 million in total, against a total project cost of about EUR 156 million, and names no co-financing lender; it notes the ADB is conducting the initial environmental examinations for all components and that two components may require resettlement. The Early Warning System record for EIB-20140457 lists no co-financiers and no related ADB project number. So: if the other agent's case is on ADB 36173-013, the EIB should not be added to it as a lender on this evidence. The caveat the main session should weigh is that both are Colombo Municipal Council wastewater operations in the same city and the physical works could overlap on the ground; the separation here rests on project numbering and on the EIB's own statement of which programme its loan sits in, not on a document saying the two ADB projects are unrelated.

One correction to the draft: it said the court injunction ordered "the seller of the site" to clean up the asbestos. The report refers to "a Court injunction against to clean up the asbestos" with the name of the party missing from the text, so who was ordered cannot be identified from it; section 5.6.4 says the complainant later pursued the matter in the national courts after obtaining the injunction.
